summary: Gives recommendations to designers of application and service protocols on using the transport port number space and when to ask IANA for a port. It is a best current practice that complements RFC 6335.

eli5.summary: Ports are like apartment numbers and there are not many. This says when you really need your own and when to share.

subtitle: Advice on when to ask IANA for a port number, and how to conserve the scarce assigned port space.

tldr.problem: Assigned transport port numbers are a limited, globally shared resource, and designers often request them when they do not need to or use them without assignment.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains the history and meaning of port numbers and recommends when to avoid requesting one, how many to ask for, which range to pick, how to handle security and versions, and when to apply.
tldr.outcome: It joins RFC 6335 as part of BCP 165, complementing but not changing the IANA procedures, and guides what port experts look for during review.

today: RFC 7605 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 165, together with RFC 6335) and has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata, so it remains the advice on requesting assigned ports.

sections.title: Purpose and Relationship to RFC 6335
sections.content:
RFC 7605 gives advice to application and service designers on using assigned transport port numbers. It gives a historical background and specific recommendations. It complements the IANA process in RFC 6335 but does not change any of its assignment procedures; the two documents together are now known as BCP 165.

The advice is meant to address concerns typically raised during Expert Review of port applications, though it does not bind those reviews. Statements using the key words are marked in the text with >>.
sections.eli5: This is a how-to guide for people who want their program to have its own official number, written to go with the existing rule book.

sections.title: How Port Numbers Evolved
sections.content:
The term 'port' first appeared in RFC 33, for the Network Control Program. Later RFCs added socket identifiers to packets so that incoming messages could be demultiplexed to the right process. RFC 61 introduced the idea of a 'well-known' port number for common services, and RFC 333 proposed using a pair of port numbers, which is the final view in RFC 793.

RFC 758 first described port numbers for TCP. It split the small number range into network-wide standard functions, host-specific functions, reserved and experimental ranges. RFC 820 first applied them to connectionless transports such as UDP. RFC 1340 increased the range from 0-255 to 0-1023 and listed TCP and UDP assignments individually. The list in RFC 1700 remained the standard until it was replaced by an online version in RFC 3232.
sections.eli5: Long ago there were only a few numbered doors for a few services. As more programs appeared, people made the list longer and wrote it down in one official place.

sections.title: What a Port Number Is
sections.content:
A port number is a 16-bit number with two purposes: demultiplexing transport endpoint associations within a host, and identifying a service. The first needs no registration. The second is what drives the need for a common registry.

RFC 6335 defines three ranges: System (also Well-Known) 0-1023, User (also Registered) 1024-49151, and Dynamic (also Private) 49152-65535. Both System and User numbers are assigned through IANA. System numbers may require privileged access (for example 'root') on some systems, though not always.

The link between a service and a port is ultimately an agreement between the two endpoints. A web server could run on port 53 for browsers that know to use it. Intermediate devices that interpret port numbers can be wrong, and the numbers may be invisible when traffic is encrypted or fragmented. A port number is also different from a service name, which is a user convenience.
sections.eli5: A port number is like an apartment number in a building: it tells the computer which program should get the message. A few numbers are officially reserved for well-known jobs.

sections.title: Why Conservation Matters
sections.content:
Assigned ports are a limited resource shared by the whole Internet. As of 2014, approximately 5850 TCP and 5570 UDP port numbers had been assigned out of a total range of 49151. Past conservation keeps the assignment rate low and avoids needing reclamation, which is practically impossible.

IANA aims to assign one port per service, including variants. Using many ports makes applications fragile when firewalls block some of them. So each requested port MUST be justified as an independently useful service.

The guiding principles are that one port can serve different functions based on in-band information, can announce Dynamic ports (as with passive-mode FTP, mDNS and portmapper), and can host copies of services told apart in-band (such as the HTTP Host field or TLS Server Name Indication). Ports are meant to tell services apart, not performance variants, replicas or payload types, and it is never appropriate to consume them to conserve IP addresses. Dynamic ports and in-band port exchange often complicate firewalls and NATs.
sections.eli5: There are only so many mailbox numbers, so each new one must be for something truly different, not just a faster copy of what exists.

sections.title: Do You Need a Port at All?
sections.content:
Designers should first ask whether an assignment is needed. Is this really a new service? Is it experimental (then use experimental ports)? Is it independently useful? Could a Dynamic port be coordinated by configuration, internal mechanisms, a related service such as FTP or SIP, or a discovery service such as portmapper or mDNS?

Several cases are directly counter-indicated: performance variations, copies of an existing service (ask whether an unmodified client of the existing service can use it), intra-machine communication, insecure versions of secure services, and differing service versions. The RFC notes that the converse, a secure version of an insecure service, can be useful. Services can also register DNS SRV names, which are assigned first-come, first-served from a much larger namespace.

Assigned numbers are typically for servers only, and they are no guarantee of exclusive use, so designers are encouraged to validate traffic by its content. Section 7.2 adds that systems rarely need several ports, and that older multi-port or large-range assignments such as X11 are not precedents.
sections.eli5: Before asking for your own number, check whether you can borrow an existing one, tell your friends the number directly, or just use a temporary one.

sections.title: Choosing a Port and Handling Versions and Security
sections.content:
A request does not have to name a number; IANA will pick one if none is requested. The most critical choice is the System or User range. The privilege distinction has blurred, so developers are advised to treat services as if they always run without privilege. Developers SHOULD NOT apply for System port numbers, and system implementers SHOULD enforce privilege for listening on them. System assignments have continued at an average of 3-4 per year over 2007-2013.

New services SHOULD support security, directly or through TLS, DTLS or TCP-AO, and insecure versions of secure services SHOULD be avoided. Security SHOULD NOT rely on assigned port distinctions alone. Version support SHOULD be built into new services in-band, and version numbers SHOULD NOT appear in the service name or description.

Assignments are specific to a transport (UDP, TCP, SCTP, DCCP). Names and descriptions across transports SHOULD match only for the same service. The suffix '-disc' is suggested for discovery services. UDP over IPv4 multi-host services SHOULD use multicast rather than broadcast, and services SHOULD NOT use UDP to avoid TCP's congestion control.
sections.eli5: Pick the ordinary kind of number, put the version inside your messages, and make sure your service is protected, because no number keeps out attackers.

sections.title: Timing, Squatting and Changes
sections.content:
IANA applications typically take up to a few weeks, with complex cases up to a month. The application must be complete and not just point to external documents. Users MUST NOT deploy implementations that use assigned port numbers before IANA assigns them, and MUST NOT default to the experimental System ports 1021 and 1022 outside a controlled environment. Specifications SHOULD use symbolic names until assignment is complete.

Squatting means using a number from the assignable range in deployed software without assignment. It is hazardous because IANA cannot track it and may legitimately assign the number to someone else. Widespread de facto use may not justify later assignment.

Assigned port numbers and names are not meant to change, and aliases are no longer considered appropriate.
sections.eli5: Do not move into an apartment before the landlord says yes. Someone else may be given that number, and then you have to move out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Port numbers do not protect against denial-of-service attacks or show that traffic should be trusted. Filtering on assigned ports is no substitute for authentication, encryption and integrity protection. TLS, DTLS or TCP-AO are encouraged; IPsec may not be usable in the same way.

Assigned port numbers are described as the antithesis of privacy, since they explicitly indicate the application. They can reveal available services to intermediate devices and help fingerprint endpoint software.
sections.eli5: A number on a door does not make a room safe. It also tells everyone passing by what is inside.
